title: Storage (Advanced)
reading:
Today's menu

By the end of this lunch you will be able to:

- Layer soft delete, versioning, point-in-time restore, immutability, replication and backup so that overwritten or deleted blobs can be recovered — or can't be destroyed at all.
- Automate a blob's journey through the access tiers, and its deletion, with lifecycle management rules.
- Lock down a storage account with firewall rules, private endpoints and private DNS, no shared keys, SAS expiration policies and customer-managed keys.
- Recognize when Data Lake Storage, SFTP, NFS or a static website fits, and what scalability targets mean for a design.
- Plan large data moves, redundancy changes and a storage account failover.

Meanwhile at Nusantara Retail

Monday, 7:40 a.m. Pak Budi forwards a message from a supplier in Surabaya: overnight, ransomware encrypted every file on their server, including the invoices they exchange with Nusantara Retail. The attackers want payment by Friday.

Ibu Sari stays calm but asks pointed questions. "Our invoices moved to Azure Storage last quarter. If someone steals a password, can they encrypt ours too? Could we get yesterday's versions back?" Finance adds a requirement of its own: the tax office can audit any invoice from the last ten years, and the auditor wants proof that nobody — not even IT — can quietly change one. Dewi, meanwhile, notices two more problems: the storage account answers requests from anywhere on the internet, and the bill shows seven-year-old invoices still sitting in the hot tier.

Today's question: how do you make Nusantara Retail's invoices recoverable, tamper-proof, cheap to keep for ten years and reachable only from its own network?

Reading

1. Layers of data protection

Lunch 07 showed how redundancy keeps copies of your data on other disks, in other zones or in another region. But redundancy copies everything, mistakes included. When ransomware overwrites an invoice, every copy is overwritten within seconds. Protection against people, scripts and malware needs different features, and they work best in layers.

Blob soft delete keeps deleted blobs for a retention period you choose (1–365 days); until it ends you can undelete them. Container soft delete does the same for whole containers — useful when someone deletes the wrong one with a single click. Blob versioning goes further: every write keeps the old content as a read-only previous version with its own version ID. Overwrite an invoice ten times and you have ten older versions to choose from. To restore one, you copy that version over the blob, and its content becomes current again.

Versioning and soft delete reinforce each other. With versioning on, deleting a blob destroys nothing: the current version simply becomes a previous version. Deleting a previous version needs the stronger Storage Blob Data Owner role, and even then the version only moves into soft delete until the retention period ends. An attacker has to get through several layers, and wait, before your data is really gone.

Point-in-time restore answers "undo everything since 2 a.m.": it rolls block blobs in a container, a set of prefixes or the whole account back to an earlier moment. It needs versioning, change feed and blob soft delete, and its restore window must be at least one day shorter than the soft delete retention. It can't bring back deleted containers (container soft delete does that) or blobs in the archive tier, and it isn't available in accounts with a hierarchical namespace or alongside immutability policies. The change feed it relies on is an ordered, read-only log of every create, update and delete, kept in the $blobchangefeed container. Read it yourself when you need to know which blobs an incident touched.

Immutable storage prevents changes instead of undoing them. It keeps data in a write once, read many (WORM) state: new blobs can be created and read, but protected data can't be modified or deleted while a time-based retention policy (1 to 146,000 days) is active or a legal hold is in place. A policy can cover a whole container (container-level) or individual blob versions (version-level, which needs versioning; an overwrite then creates a new version and the protected one stays untouched). A new policy starts unlocked, which is meant for short tests: it already blocks deletes, but you can still shorten or delete the policy itself. Once you lock it, you can only lengthen the period, and not even a subscription Owner can delete the protected blobs — or the account that holds them — before it ends. Test unlocked, lock deliberately.

Object replication asynchronously copies block blobs from a container in one account to a container in another, often in another region. It needs versioning on both sides and change feed on the source. Unlike geo-redundancy, the copy is a separate account you can read at any time, with its own tier, rules and permissions. New accounts block replication to other Microsoft Entra tenants by default.

Two safety nets sit outside the account. Azure Backup offers operational backup for blobs and a vaulted backup that copies data into a Backup vault, which survives even the deletion of the storage account (Lunch 17). A CanNotDelete resource lock (Lunch 18) stops the account from being deleted by accident — and if it happens anyway, a deleted account can often be recovered within 14 days, as long as nobody has reused its name.

Feature | Protects against | How you recover | Good to know
Blob soft delete | Deleted blobs and versions | Undelete within 1–365 days | Deleted data is billed until the period ends
Container soft delete | A deleted container | Restore the container | Doesn't cover single blobs
Versioning | Overwrites and deletes | Copy a previous version over the blob | Every version is billed; tidy up with lifecycle rules
Point-in-time restore | Mass changes ("undo last night") | Restore block blobs to a moment | Needs versioning, change feed and soft delete
Change feed | Nothing by itself — it's the audit trail | Read which blobs changed, and when | Log blobs are billed as storage
Immutability (WORM) | Anyone changing or deleting data | Nothing to recover — the change is refused | Locked policies can't be shortened or removed
Object replication | Losing an account or region | Read the copy in the other account | Asynchronous; block blobs only
Vaulted backup | Account deletion, ransomware, rogue admins | Restore from the Backup vault | Covered in Lunch 17

2. Lifecycle management: let rules do the tiering

Invoices follow a predictable life: busy for a month, checked now and then for a quarter, rarely opened after the first year, deleted after ten. Moving millions of them by hand would be a full-time job. A lifecycle management policy does it for you: a JSON document of up to 100 rules that the platform runs once a day.

Each rule has filters — blob types, up to ten name prefixes that start with the container name, or blob index tags — and actions for the current version (baseBlob), previous versions (version) and snapshots. The actions are tierToCool, tierToCold, tierToArchive and delete, each triggered by a condition such as daysAfterModificationGreaterThan, daysAfterCreationGreaterThan or daysAfterLastAccessTimeGreaterThan (which needs last access time tracking). This is the heart of the rule you deploy in the lab:

"filters": { "blobTypes": [ "blockBlob" ], "prefixMatch": [ "invoices/" ] },
"actions": {
  "baseBlob": {
    "tierToCool":    { "daysAfterModificationGreaterThan": 30 },
    "tierToCold":    { "daysAfterModificationGreaterThan": 90 },
    "tierToArchive": { "daysAfterModificationGreaterThan": 365, "daysAfterLastTierChangeGreaterThan": 7 },
    "delete":        { "daysAfterModificationGreaterThan": 3650 }
  },
  "version": {
    "tierToCold": { "daysAfterCreationGreaterThan": 30 },
    "delete":     { "daysAfterCreationGreaterThan": 365 }
  }
}

A few details decide whether such a rule saves money or causes surprises:

- Respect the minimum storage durations. Space the steps at least 30 days apart after cool, 90 after cold and 180 after archive, or you pay early deletion charges. The rule above keeps each invoice in every tier long enough.
- Include previous versions. Lifecycle management doesn't delete a current version while it still has previous versions or snapshots, so a delete rule for old invoices needs a matching version action.
- Mind the redundancy. The archive tier isn't available on ZRS, GZRS or RA-GZRS accounts, so tierToArchive can't apply there.
- Avoid ping-pong. daysAfterLastTierChangeGreaterThan stops a freshly rehydrated invoice from being archived again the next morning. With last access time tracking, enableAutoTierToHotFromCool moves a cool blob back to hot when someone reads it.
- Be patient. A new or changed policy can take up to 24 hours to act, and immutable blobs are never deleted while their retention is active.

If you'd rather not write rules at all, the smart tier from Lunch 07 moves blobs between hot, cool and cold for you.

Tip: Lifecycle rules are free to run, but every tier change is billed as a write operation. For millions of tiny files, those operations can cost more than the storage they save — model it in the pricing calculator first, or bundle small files into larger archives before they age.

3. Locking the doors: network, keys and encryption

By default a storage account's public endpoint accepts connections from any network; your data is safe only because every request must be authorized. Advanced designs add network controls on top.

The storage firewall has three settings for public network access: enabled from all networks, enabled from selected virtual networks and IP addresses, or Disabled. With selected networks you add IP rules for public addresses (up to 400), virtual network rules for subnets that use a service endpoint, resource instance rules for specific Azure resources, and the trusted Microsoft services exception for services such as Azure Backup. IP rules don't work for clients in the same Azure region as the account, because those use private Azure addresses — use virtual network rules or private endpoints for them. A request blocked by the firewall gets 403 AuthorizationFailure, even with valid credentials.

There are two ways to bring a virtual network closer to storage:

| Service endpoint | Private endpoint
What it does | Lets a subnet reach the account's public endpoint over the Azure backbone, identified as that subnet | Gives the account a private IP address on a network interface in your subnet
DNS changes | None | A private DNS zone such as privatelink.blob.core.windows.net
Reachable from peered networks and on-premises | No, only from enabled subnets | Yes, over peering, VPN or ExpressRoute — once DNS is right
Works when public network access is Disabled | No | Yes
Granularity | Per subnet and service (Microsoft.Storage) | Per account and sub-resource (blob, dfs, file, queue, table, web)
Cost | Free | Hourly charge plus per-GB data processing

A private endpoint only helps if clients find it. Applications keep using the normal name, such as stnusa24abcde.blob.core.windows.net. Public DNS answers with a CNAME to stnusa24abcde.privatelink.blob.core.windows.net. Inside a virtual network that is linked to a private DNS zone with that name, the zone answers with the endpoint's private IP address; everywhere else, the name resolves to the public IP address as before. A DNS zone group on the private endpoint keeps that A record up to date for you.

Warning: The most common private endpoint mistake is forgetting DNS. Without a private DNS zone linked to the client's virtual network (or a matching record on your own DNS servers), clients still resolve the public IP address — and once public access is disabled, they fail with 403 AuthorizationFailure. Check with nslookup from inside the network before you switch public access off.

Identity controls tighten things further. Disallowing Shared Key authorization (--allow-shared-key-access false) stops anyone using the account keys, and with them every service SAS and account SAS; Microsoft Entra ID requests and user delegation SAS keep working. Check your tools first — some older tools and a few Azure Files scenarios still depend on keys. A SAS expiration policy (--sas-expiration-period) sets a recommended maximum lifetime for new SAS tokens, and either logs or blocks tokens that exceed it.

Everything in Azure Storage is encrypted at rest with 256-bit AES, using Microsoft-managed keys by default. With customer-managed keys you keep the key in Azure Key Vault or Managed HSM (soft delete and purge protection required); the account reads it through a managed identity and can follow new key versions automatically. Disable or delete that key and every read and write fails — a deliberate kill switch, and a reason to protect the key vault as carefully as the data. Infrastructure encryption adds a second layer, but only if you enable it when you create the account.

Microsoft Defender for Storage (Lunch 15) watches the data plane: unusual access patterns, suspicious uploads and signs of data exfiltration. Its optional malware scanning checks new blobs as they arrive and is billed per gigabyte scanned, while sensitive data threat detection focuses alerts on accounts holding personal or financial data.

4. Special-purpose storage and scale

Data Lake Storage is a storage account with a hierarchical namespace (HNS). Folders become real directories, so renaming or deleting one is a single atomic operation instead of millions of blob copies, and you can set POSIX-like access control lists per directory and file through the dfs endpoint. Analytics engines such as Microsoft Fabric and Azure Databricks expect it. Some blob features, including point-in-time restore and object replication, aren't available with HNS, and switching an existing account to HNS is a one-way upgrade — check the feature support table first.

Two protocols ride on top of HNS. SFTP lets suppliers upload files with a normal SFTP client, using local users with an SSH key or password that are separate from Entra ID; it's billed per hour while enabled, so switch it off when unused. NFS 3.0 for blobs lets Linux and HPC workloads mount a container. NFS requests can't be authorized with keys or Entra ID, so the account must accept traffic only from virtual networks, through service endpoints or private endpoints. (Azure Files offers NFS 4.1 on its SSD tier.)

A static website serves HTML, CSS and images straight from a special $web container on its own web endpoint, with an index document and a custom 404 page — no web server needed. Content in $web is always readable anonymously, even when anonymous access is disallowed elsewhere in the account. For a custom domain with HTTPS, put Azure Front Door in front of it.

Finally, scalability targets describe how much one account handles before throttling: by default up to 5 PiB, and up to 40,000 requests per second in larger regions such as Southeast Asia (20,000 in others), with similar limits on throughput. When an account or one of its partitions is pushed too hard, Azure Storage returns 503 Server Busy or 500 Operation Timeout; clients should retry with exponential back-off. Very busy workloads spread data across several accounts — by default you can create 250 per region per subscription, and up to 1,000 on request.

5. Moving data at scale and surviving a region

Lunch 07 introduced AzCopy and Data Box for one-off copies. At scale, the question becomes how to keep moving data and how to fail over safely.

Tool | Moves data | Best for | Watch out for
azcopy sync | Online, scripted, incremental | Mirroring a folder or container on a schedule | --delete-destination true deletes extra files at the target
Azure Storage Mover | Online, managed from Azure | Migrating SMB or NFS shares, project by project | Needs an agent near on-premises sources
Azure Data Box | Offline, shipped device | Tens to hundreds of terabytes over a slow line | Shipping takes days; order early
Azure File Sync | Online, continuous, two-way | Branch file servers with a local cache (cloud tiering) | Not supported with customer-managed failover
Object replication | Online, continuous, one-way | Readable copies of block blobs in another region | Asynchronous: the copy lags behind

Redundancy can change later. Switching between LRS and GRS (or RA-GRS) is a simple update, although adding geo-redundancy costs a one-time copy to the secondary region. Adding zones — LRS to ZRS, or GRS to GZRS — needs a conversion that Microsoft runs in the background without a completion SLA, or a manual copy to a new account. Archived blobs get in the way of both: move or rehydrate them first.

For geo-redundant accounts you can start a failover yourself:

Failover type | When to use it | Data loss | Afterwards
Customer-managed planned failover | Both regions are healthy: disaster recovery drills, or problems with a service in the primary | None — it waits for replication to catch up | The regions swap roles and geo-redundancy keeps working
Customer-managed (unplanned) failover | The primary endpoint is unavailable | Writes after the Last Sync Time | The account is LRS in the new primary; re-enable geo-redundancy, which copies everything again
Microsoft-managed failover | A whole region is lost | Possible | Microsoft decides when; don't build your plan around it

A failover usually completes within an hour, and clients keep the same endpoint names. Before an unplanned failover, check how much you might lose with az storage account show --name <account> --expand geoReplicationStats --query geoReplicationStats.lastSyncTime. Not every account can fail over — Azure File Sync, for example, isn't supported — so check the documentation's list of unsupported features before you depend on it.

6. How it fits together for Nusantara Retail

Back to Ibu Sari's questions. This is the design Dewi presents for the invoices, which stay in Indonesia Central:

- Recoverable: the working account for current invoices (general-purpose v2, ZRS) gets versioning, 14 days of blob and container soft delete, change feed and seven days of point-in-time restore. Monday's ransomware scenario becomes "restore to 2 a.m." instead of "pay by Friday".
- Tamper-proof: when a tax year closes, its invoices are copied to a second ZRS account, into a container with a locked ten-year time-based retention policy — tested unlocked first, with finance signing off on the period. A separate account is needed anyway, because immutability and point-in-time restore can't share one.
- Cheap for ten years: lifecycle rules move invoices to cool after 30 days and cold after 90. Because ZRS can't archive, object replication sends finished invoices to an LRS account in Southeast Asia, where a rule archives them — once the compliance team confirms that a copy may leave Indonesia.
- Private: blob private endpoints in the hub network from Lunch 25, a linked privatelink.blob.core.windows.net zone, public network access Disabled, Shared Key disallowed, and the storefront reading data with a managed identity.
- Watched: Defender for Storage with malware scanning on the separate SFTP-enabled account where suppliers drop their files, and a vaulted backup of the invoice containers.

Pause and think: An attacker steals Dewi's account, which holds the Owner role on the subscription. Which of these protections can they simply switch off or delete — soft delete, versioning, an unlocked policy, a locked policy, the vaulted backup — and which ones still save the 2025 invoices?

In the lab you build the protection layers on a small scale, rescue invoices from a simulated attack and then close the public door. Next, Lunch 25 builds the hub-and-spoke network where private endpoints like this one live.

Field notes from Stefanus

Ask who can switch it off. For every protection layer on a storage account, I ask one question in design reviews: who can turn this off, and how fast? Soft delete, versioning and an unlocked retention policy all rescue you from accidents, but anyone with the Owner role can disable them in a few clicks — so I treat them as undo buttons, not as protection against a stolen admin account. Only a locked policy or a backup held under separate permissions answers that threat, and I want someone outside IT to sign off before anything gets locked. Then I book a restore drill: overwrite a test file, delete a test container and time how long it takes to get both back. Protection you have never restored from is a hope, not a plan.

Go further

- Microsoft Learn: Data protection overview (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/storage/blobs/data-protection-overview) — which protection options to combine for each scenario, with a handy comparison table.
- Microsoft Learn: Store business-critical blob data with immutable storage (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/storage/blobs/immutable-storage-overview) — container-level vs version-level policies, locking and legal holds.
- Microsoft Learn: Use private endpoints for Azure Storage (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/storage/common/storage-private-endpoints) — DNS zones per sub-resource and how name resolution changes.
- Microsoft Learn: Azure storage disaster recovery planning and failover (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/storage/common/storage-disaster-recovery-guidance) — failover types, Last Sync Time and unsupported features.

quiz.q: Overnight, a compromised script overwrote 2,000 invoices in a container that has versioning, change feed, soft delete and point-in-time restore enabled. What is the fastest way back?
quiz.a: Run a point-in-time restore of that container (or prefix) to a moment before the script started. It uses the versions and the change feed to roll every affected block blob back in one operation, instead of you promoting 2,000 previous versions one by one.

quiz.q: Finance wants the 2025 invoices undeletable for ten years, even by administrators, but isn't sure the period is right. How do you proceed?
quiz.a: Create a time-based retention policy and test it unlocked, where it can still be shortened or deleted. Lock it only after finance confirms the period, because a locked policy can only be extended — and it then blocks deleting the protected blobs and the account until the period ends.

quiz.q: Dewi created a private endpoint for blob storage, but nslookup from a VM in the same virtual network still returns a public IP address. What's missing?
quiz.a: The private DNS zone privatelink.blob.core.windows.net isn't linked to that virtual network (or has no A record for the account, for example because the DNS zone group is missing). Without it, the CNAME to the privatelink name falls through to public DNS.

quiz.q: A colleague's lifecycle rule moves invoices to cool after 10 days and to archive after 20 days. What's wrong with it?
quiz.a: It ignores the minimum storage durations. Each blob leaves cool after only 10 of its 30 days, so you pay an early deletion charge on every one. Space the steps at least as far apart as each tier's minimum (30 days for cool, 90 for cold, 180 for archive).

quiz.q: The primary region of a GRS account becomes unavailable and you start a customer-managed failover. What should you tell the business to expect?
quiz.a: Writes made after the Last Sync Time may be lost, because replication to the secondary is asynchronous. After failover the account is LRS in the new primary region until you re-enable geo-redundancy, which copies all data again.

takeaways: Redundancy copies mistakes; versioning, soft delete, point-in-time restore and backup let you undo them, and a locked immutability policy stops them from happening at all.
Lifecycle rules tier and delete data automatically — design them around minimum storage durations, and include previous versions.
A private endpoint gives the account a private IP address, but only DNS makes clients use it: link the privatelink.blob.core.windows.net zone, test, then disable public network access.
Disallow Shared Key, cap SAS lifetimes, and use customer-managed keys and Defender for Storage when the data is sensitive.
Plan for scale and disasters: pick the right bulk-transfer tool, know which redundancy changes need a conversion, and check Last Sync Time before an unplanned failover.

lab.title: Ransomware-proof invoices
lab.text: What you'll build A supplier of Nusantara Retail was hit by ransomware. You make sure the same attack can't cost Nusantara its invoices: you switch on versioning, soft delete and change feed, then play the attacker — overwrite an invoice, delete another, even delete the whole container — and recover everything. You add a ten-year lifecycle policy and a write-once retention policy for a closed tax year. Finally, you give the account a private endpoint and a private DNS zone, prove from a VM inside the network that the account's name now resolves to a private IP address, and switch off public network access. Before you start - An Azure subscription where you can create resources and assign roles (Owner, or Contributor plus User Access Administrator) — see Lab 01 (https://stefpin.github.io/azure-fundamentals-lunches/en/labs/01-before-you-begin.html). - Azure Cloud Shell (Bash) — open shell.azure.com. Nothing to install. - Read the Lunch 24 reading (https://stefpin.github.io/azure-fundamentals-lunches/en/lunches/24-storage-advanced.html) first; this lab assumes you know what versions, soft delete, immutability and private endpoints are. - Get the lab files and load the shared settings (run this block again whenever Cloud Shell restarts): git clone https://github.com/stefpin/azure-fundamentals-lunches.git # first time only cd azure-fundamentals-lunches/labs/24-storage-advanced source ../common/config.sh RG=$(rg_name 24) ACCOUNT="stnusa24${SUFFIX}" VNET=vnet-nusa-lab24 ZONE=privatelink.blob.core.windows.net ACCOUNT_ID=$(az storage account show --name "$ACCOUNT" --resource-group "$RG" --query id --output tsv 2>/dev/null) mkdir -p work echo "Resource group: $RG Storage account: $ACCOUNT" - Create the starting point — a virtual network with two subnets, a NAT gateway and a small Linux VM without a public IP address. It takes about 5 minutes; read section 3 of the lunch while you wait: bash setup.sh The VM is only there to test DNS and network paths from inside the virtual network. It has no public IP and no inbound rules; you reach it through Run Command, which needs outbound HTTPS to return its output — that's why setup.sh adds a NAT gateway (new subnets have no default outbound internet access). Important: The VM, the NAT gateway and the private endpoint are billed by the hour. Finish with the Clean up section, even if you stop halfway — and never lock the retention policy in Task 6, or the account can't be deleted for days. Choose your mode Mode | For you if… | How Guided | you want every step explained | follow Tasks 1–9 below Challenge | you already know the basics | run bash setup.sh, read only the Challenge brief, build it your way, then run bash verify.sh Task 1 · Create the invoice account and give yourself a data role The account is general-purpose v2 with locally redundant storage (cheap, and it supports the archive tier your lifecycle rule uses), TLS 1.2 and no anonymous access. You work with blob data through your Microsoft Entra identity, so you need a data role. az storage account create \ --name "$ACCOUNT" \ --resource-group "$RG" \ --location "$LOCATION" \ --kind StorageV2 \ --sku Standard_LRS \ --min-tls-version TLS1_2 \ --allow-blob-public-access false \ --https-only true \ --output none ACCOUNT_ID=$(az storage account show --name "$ACCOUNT" --resource-group "$RG" --query id --output tsv) az role assignment create \ --assignee-object-id "$(my_object_id)" \ --assignee-principal-type User \ --role "Storage Blob Data Contributor" \ --scope "$ACCOUNT_ID" \ --output none wait_until "your data role to take effect" 600 \ az storage container list --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --auth-mode login \ && echo "Data role is active." Checkpoint: Data role is active. is printed, and az role assignment list --assignee "$(my_object_id)" --scope "$ACCOUNT_ID" --query "[].roleDefinitionName" --output tsv shows Storage Blob Data Contributor. Task 2 · Switch on the protection layers One command enables versioning, 14 days of soft delete for blobs and for containers, and the change feed: az storage account blob-service-properties update \ --account-name "$ACCOUNT" \ --resource-group "$RG" \ --enable-versioning true \ --enable-delete-retention true --delete-retention-days 14 \ --enable-container-delete-retention true --container-delete-retention-days 14 \ --enable-change-feed true \ --output none You leave point-in-time restore off on purpose: it can't be combined with the immutability policy you add in Task 6. (Point-in-time restore is a stretch goal, on a separate account.) Tip: Prefer the portal? Storage account › Data management › Data protection. Tick versioning, soft delete for blobs and containers (14 days) and blob change feed, then Save. Checkpoint: this prints True, 14, 14, True: az storage account blob-service-properties show --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --resource-group "$RG" \ --query "{versioning:isVersioningEnabled, blobSoftDeleteDays:deleteRetentionPolicy.days, containerSoftDeleteDays:containerDeleteRetentionPolicy.days, changeFeed:changeFeed.enabled}" \ --output table Task 3 · Upload invoices, play the ransomware, restore a version Create the invoices container and upload two invoices: az storage container create --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --name invoices --auth-mode login --output none for f in sample-files/INV-2026-0042.txt sample-files/INV-2026-0043.txt; do az storage blob upload --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --container-name invoices \ --name "$(basename "$f")" --file "$f" --auth-mode login --output none done Now be the attacker. Ransomware doesn't need to delete anything — it just overwrites files with encrypted garbage: printf 'ENCRYPTED BY RANSOMWARE - pay by Friday to get your invoice back\n' > work/INV-2026-0042.txt az storage blob upload --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --container-name invoices --name INV-2026-0042.txt \ --file work/INV-2026-0042.txt --overwrite --auth-mode login --output none rm -f work/check.txt az storage blob download --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --container-name invoices --name INV-2026-0042.txt \ --file work/check.txt --auth-mode login --output none cat work/check.txt Without versioning, that invoice would be gone. List its versions — each write created one, with a timestamp as its ID: az storage blob list --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --container-name invoices --include v --prefix INV-2026-0042 \ --auth-mode login --query "[].{name:name, versionId:versionId, current:isCurrentVersion}" --output table The oldest version holds the original invoice. Read it, then promote it by copying it over the current blob: ORIGINAL=$(az storage blob list --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --container-name invoices --include v \ --prefix INV-2026-0042.txt --auth-mode login \ --query "sort_by([?name=='INV-2026-0042.txt'], &versionId)[0].versionId" --output tsv) echo "Original version: $ORIGINAL" rm -f work/original.txt az storage blob download --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --container-name invoices --name INV-2026-0042.txt \ --version-id "$ORIGINAL" --file work/original.txt --auth-mode login --output none head -n 3 work/original.txt az storage blob copy start --account-name "$ACCOUNT" \ --destination-container invoices --destination-blob INV-2026-0042.txt \ --source-uri "https://${ACCOUNT}.blob.core.windows.net/invoices/INV-2026-0042.txt?versionId=${ORIGINAL}" \ --auth-mode login --output none The copy creates a new current version with the original content; the encrypted one stays behind as a previous version, which a lifecycle rule (Task 5) cleans up later. Tip: Prefer the portal? Storage browser › invoices › INV-2026-0042.txt › Versions tab › select the oldest version › Make current version. It does the same copy for you. Checkpoint: download the blob again (the download and cat commands above) — the first line reads PT NUSANTARA RETAIL - INVOICE INV-2026-0042, and the version list now shows three versions. Task 4 · Delete an invoice, then the whole container — and get both back Delete the second invoice and look at the container: az storage blob delete --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --container-name invoices --name INV-2026-0043.txt \ --auth-mode login --output none az storage blob list --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --container-name invoices --auth-mode login --query "[].name" --output tsv az storage blob list --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --container-name invoices --include v --prefix INV-2026-0043 \ --auth-mode login --query "[].{name:name, versionId:versionId, current:isCurrentVersion}" --output table The invoice is missing from the normal listing, but its version is still there: with versioning on, a delete only turns the current version into a previous one. (az storage blob undelete restores soft-deleted versions; it doesn't bring back a current version, so promoting is the way here.) Promote the newest version, exactly as in Task 3: LATEST=$(az storage blob list --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --container-name invoices --include v \ --prefix INV-2026-0043.txt --auth-mode login \ --query "sort_by([?name=='INV-2026-0043.txt'], &versionId)[-1].versionId" --output tsv) az storage blob copy start --account-name "$ACCOUNT" \ --destination-container invoices --destination-blob INV-2026-0043.txt \ --source-uri "https://${ACCOUNT}.blob.core.windows.net/invoices/INV-2026-0043.txt?versionId=${LATEST}" \ --auth-mode login --output none Now something bigger: someone deletes the whole container. Container soft delete keeps it for 14 days. az storage container delete --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --name invoices --auth-mode login --output none az storage container list --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --include-deleted --auth-mode login \ --query "[?deleted].{name:name, version:version}" --output table DELETED_VERSION=$(az storage container list --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --include-deleted --auth-mode login \ --query "[?name=='invoices' && deleted] | [0].version" --output tsv) az storage container restore --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --name invoices \ --deleted-version "$DELETED_VERSION" --auth-mode login --output none If the restore says The specified container is being deleted, wait 30 seconds and run the last command again. Checkpoint: az storage blob list --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --container-name invoices --auth-mode login --query "[].name" --output tsv lists both invoices again — the container came back with its blobs and their versions. Task 5 · Deploy a ten-year lifecycle policy Look at lifecycle-policy.json: one rule for block blobs whose names start with invoices/ (the container name). Current versions move to cool after 30 days, cold after 90 and archive after a year — but not within 7 days of a tier change, so a rehydrated invoice isn't archived again straight away — and are deleted after 3,650 days. Previous versions move to cold after 30 days and are deleted after a year, so ransomware leftovers don't pile up. cat lifecycle-policy.json az storage account management-policy create --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --resource-group "$RG" \ --policy @lifecycle-policy.json --output none The steps are spaced so that every invoice stays in each tier at least as long as that tier's minimum storage duration (30, 90 and 180 days), so the rule never causes early deletion charges. The platform runs lifecycle rules once a day, and a new policy can take up to 24 hours to start — your minutes-old invoices won't move today. Tip: Prefer the portal? Storage account › Data management › Lifecycle management › Add a rule. After saving, open Code view to see the same JSON. Checkpoint: this shows the rule invoices-ten-years, enabled, with 30, 90, 365 and 3650: az storage account management-policy show --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --resource-group "$RG" \ --query "policy.rules[].{rule:name, enabled:enabled, cool:definition.actions.baseBlob.tierToCool.daysAfterModificationGreaterThan, cold:definition.actions.baseBlob.tierToCold.daysAfterModificationGreaterThan, archive:definition.actions.baseBlob.tierToArchive.daysAfterModificationGreaterThan, delete:definition.actions.baseBlob.delete.daysAfterModificationGreaterThan}" \ --output table Task 6 · Make a closed tax year immutable Tax year 2025 is closed; its invoices must not change. Create a container for it, upload the invoice, and add a time-based retention policy of one day (in real life: ten years, or 3,650 days): az storage container create --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --name invoices-2025 --auth-mode login --output none az storage blob upload --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --container-name invoices-2025 --name INV-2025-0999.txt \ --file sample-files/INV-2025-0999.txt --auth-mode login --output none az storage container immutability-policy create --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --resource-group "$RG" \ --container-name invoices-2025 --period 1 --output none az storage container immutability-policy show --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --resource-group "$RG" \ --container-name invoices-2025 --query "{state:state, days:immutabilityPeriodSinceCreationInDays}" --output table Give the policy a moment to take effect, then try to delete the invoice — as an attacker with your permissions would: sleep 45 az storage blob delete --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --container-name invoices-2025 --name INV-2025-0999.txt \ --auth-mode login The delete is refused with BlobImmutableDueToPolicy (HTTP 409), even though you have full data access. The policy protects each blob for one day after it was created; after that, the blob can be deleted but still not changed. Locked vs unlocked. Your policy is Unlocked: it already blocks deletes and changes, but you can still shorten it or remove it. That makes it right for testing — and it's why cleanup.sh can tidy up after this lab. A Locked policy (az storage container immutability-policy lock) can only be extended, up to five times, and can never be deleted. While locked, the protected blobs can't be deleted before their period ends, and the storage account can't be deleted while the container exists. That is what an auditor wants for ten years of invoices — and why you don't lock it in a lab. Tip: Prefer the portal? Container invoices-2025 › Settings › Access policy › Immutable blob storage › Add policy › Time-based retention, 1 day. Checkpoint: the show command prints Unlocked and 1, and the delete fails with This operation is not permitted as the blob is immutable due to a policy. Task 7 · Give the account a private endpoint and a private DNS zone A private endpoint puts a network interface for the account's blob service into snet-pe. Because you own the account, the connection is approved automatically. az network private-endpoint create \ --resource-group "$RG" \ --name pe-stnusa24-blob \ --location "$LOCATION" \ --vnet-name "$VNET" \ --subnet snet-pe \ --private-connection-resource-id "$ACCOUNT_ID" \ --group-id blob \ --connection-name pec-stnusa24-blob \ --output none Without DNS, nobody would use it. Create the private DNS zone, link it to the virtual network, and add a DNS zone group to the endpoint, which writes (and maintains) the A record for your account in the zone: az network private-dns zone create --resource-group "$RG" --name "$ZONE" --output none az network private-dns link vnet create --resource-group "$RG" --zone-name "$ZONE" \ --name link-vnet-nusa-lab24 --virtual-network "$VNET" --registration-enabled false --output none az network private-endpoint dns-zone-group create --resource-group "$RG" --endpoint-name pe-stnusa24-blob \ --name default --private-dns-zone "$ZONE" --zone-name blob --output none az network private-dns record-set a list --resource-group "$RG" --zone-name "$ZONE" \ --query "[].{name:name, ip:aRecords[0].ipv4Address}" --output table Tip: Prefer the portal? Storage account › Security + networking › Networking › Private endpoints › + Private endpoint. Choose sub-resource blob, subnet snet-pe, and Integrate with private DNS zone: Yes — the portal creates the zone, the link and the zone group for you. Checkpoint: the record list shows your account name with an address in 10.24.2.0/24 (usually 10.24.2.4), and az network private-endpoint show --resource-group "$RG" --name pe-stnusa24-blob --query "privateLinkServiceConnections[0].privateLinkServiceConnectionState.status" --output tsv prints Approved. Task 8 · Compare DNS answers: Cloud Shell vs inside the network From Cloud Shell, which runs on the internet side: nslookup "${ACCOUNT}.blob.core.windows.net" You see a chain of aliases — first .privatelink.blob.core.windows.net, then a public storage host name — and a public IP address. Cloud Shell isn't in vnet-nusa-lab24, so the private zone doesn't apply to it. Now ask the same question from vm-dns-1, inside the virtual network. Run Command takes 20–60 seconds: az vm run-command invoke --resource-group "$RG" --name vm-dns-1 --command-id RunShellScript \ --scripts "nslookup ${ACCOUNT}.blob.core.windows.net || getent hosts ${ACCOUNT}.blob.core.windows.net" \ --query "value[0].message" --output tsv Same name, same alias to privatelink, but this time the linked private DNS zone answers with 10.24.2.4 (or whichever address Task 7 showed). Applications don't change their connection strings at all — DNS does the redirection. Checkpoint: Cloud Shell shows a public address; the VM shows your private endpoint's 10.24.2.x address. Task 9 · Close the public door — data-plane work first Disabling public network access blocks every request that reaches the public endpoint, including yours from Cloud Shell and the portal's Storage browser. Management (control-plane) operations through Azure Resource Manager keep working, but anything that touches blob data must now come through the private endpoint. So finish data-plane tasks first. Here, that's one more: a read-only user delegation SAS for an invoice, valid for one hour, which you'll use to test both network paths. (Generating it asks the blob endpoint for a user delegation key — a data-plane call that would fail after the lockdown.) EXPIRY=$(date -u -d "+1 hour" '+%Y-%m-%dT%H:%MZ') SAS_URL=$(az storage blob generate-sas --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --container-name invoices \ --name INV-2026-0042.txt --permissions r --expiry "$EXPIRY" --https-only \ --auth-mode login --as-user --full-uri --output tsv) curl -s -o /dev/null -w "Cloud Shell, public access on: HTTP %{http_code}\n" "$SAS_URL" Now close the door: az storage account update --name "$ACCOUNT" --resource-group "$RG" \ --public-network-access Disabled --output none az storage account show --name "$ACCOUNT" --resource-group "$RG" \ --query "{publicNetworkAccess:publicNetworkAccess, defaultAction:networkRuleSet.defaultAction}" --output table Test from Cloud Shell (if you still get 200, wait a minute — network changes take a moment): curl -s -o work/blocked.xml -w "Cloud Shell, public access Disabled: HTTP %{http_code}\n" "$SAS_URL" grep -o '[^<]*' work/blocked.xml az storage blob list --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --container-name invoices --auth-mode login --output table Both fail: curl gets 403 with AuthorizationFailure, and the CLI reports This request is not authorized to perform this operation. — valid credentials, wrong network. Now the same SAS URL from the VM, through the private endpoint: az vm run-command invoke --resource-group "$RG" --name vm-dns-1 --command-id RunShellScript \ --scripts "curl -s -w '\nHTTP %{http_code}\n' '${SAS_URL}'" \ --query "value[0].message" --output tsv The invoice comes back with HTTP 200. Same URL, same SAS — the only difference is the network path. Tip: Prefer the portal? Storage account › Security + networking › Networking › Public network access › Disabled › Save. Then open Storage browser and see the error for yourself. Checkpoint: Cloud Shell gets 403 / AuthorizationFailure; the VM gets the invoice text and HTTP 200. Break it and fix it A colleague "tidies up" the private DNS zone and removes its link to the virtual network. Simulate it: az network private-dns link vnet delete --resource-group "$RG" --zone-name "$ZONE" \ --name link-vnet-nusa-lab24 --yes sleep 60 az vm run-command invoke --resource-group "$RG" --name vm-dns-1 --command-id RunShellScript \ --scripts "resolvectl flush-caches; nslookup ${ACCOUNT}.blob.core.windows.net; curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'HTTP %{http_code}\n' '${SAS_URL}'" \ --query "value[0].message" --output tsv Symptom: the VM now resolves the public IP address, and the request fails with HTTP 403. The private endpoint still exists and is still approved — but without the zone link, the VM's DNS answers send it to the public endpoint (out through the NAT gateway), which you disabled in Task 9. (If more than an hour has passed, the SAS has expired and you get 403 anyway; the nslookup answer alone proves the point.) Hint: the fix Recreate the link exactly as in Task 7, wait a minute, and run the same Run Command again: az network private-dns link vnet create --resource-group "$RG" --zone-name "$ZONE" \ --name link-vnet-nusa-lab24 --virtual-network "$VNET" --registration-enabled false --output none The VM resolves 10.24.2.x again and gets HTTP 200. Lesson: a private endpoint is only half the job — clients must resolve the name through a zone that is linked to their network (or through DNS servers that forward to it). Verify your work bash verify.sh Every check should say PASS. If one fails, the message tells you which task to revisit. verify.sh uses only management calls, so it works even though public network access is now Disabled. Clean up (do not skip!) bash cleanup.sh unset SAS_URL This removes the unlocked retention policy on invoices-2025, deletes the resource group rg-lunch24- (with the storage account, private endpoint, private DNS zone, VM, NAT gateway and virtual network) and the local work/ folder. Deletion continues in the background for a few minutes. If you locked the policy A locked policy can't be removed, so the storage account (and its resource group) survives until the retention period ends — one day after each blob was created, if you used --period 1. cleanup.sh still deletes everything else. After the period ends: 1. Turn public network access back on: az storage account update --name "$ACCOUNT" --resource-group "$RG" --public-network-access Enabled --default-action Allow 2. Empty invoices-2025: delete its blobs and their previous versions (deleting versions needs Storage Blob Data Owner, which you can assign yourself as in Task 1). 3. Delete the container through the control plane: az storage container-rm delete --storage-account "$ACCOUNT" --resource-group "$RG" --name invoices-2025 --yes 4. Run bash cleanup.sh again. If Azure still refuses, read the container-level WORM documentation or open a support request. A few kilobytes in an LRS account cost almost nothing in the meantime. (Do this before Task 9, or turn public access back on for a moment.) - Point-in-time restore: create a second account (not this one — PITR and immutability can't share an account), enable point-in-time restore with 6 days and soft delete with 7, change a few blobs, then use Containers › Restore containers in the portal to roll them back. - Read the change feed: before Task 9, list az storage blob list --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --container-name '$blobchangefeed' --auth-mode login --query "[].name" --output tsv. What do both accounts need first? Challenge brief Run bash setup.sh first, then build the following, any way you like (portal, CLI, Bicep), in rg-lunch24-: 1. A general-purpose v2 storage account named stnusa24 (LRS is fine). 2. Blob versioning, blob soft delete and container soft delete (at least 7 days each), and change feed — all enabled. 3. Recovery practice (prove it to yourself; verify.sh can't check it): overwrite an invoice and restore its original version; delete an invoice and bring it back; delete a container and restore it. 4. An enabled lifecycle rule that moves blobs to cooler tiers and deletes them at the end of their life (for example from lifecycle-policy.json). 5. A container invoices-2025 with a time-based retention policy that stays unlocked. 6. A private endpoint for the blob sub-resource in snet-pe of vnet-nusa-lab24, and a private DNS zone privatelink.blob.core.windows.net in the same resource group, linked to vnet-nusa-lab24, with an A record for the account. From vm-dns-1, the account name resolves to a 10.24.2.x address. 7. Public network access Disabled — after all your data-plane work is done. Then run bash verify.sh. Stuck?
